'''Anthony Weston''' is an American writer, teacher, and philosopher.

==Life==
Weston was born in 1954 and grew up in the [[Sauk County, Wisconsin|Sauk County]] region of southwestern Wisconsin, country identified with the [[Conservation movement|conservationist]] [[Aldo Leopold]] (in his [[Sand County Almanac]]) and the architect and [[visionary]] [[Frank Lloyd Wright]], a strong influence on his father's family.<ref>Edgar Tafel, ''About Wright: An Album of Recollections about Frank Lloyd Wright by Those Who Knew Him'' (Wiley, 1993), pp. 97–99; William Drennan, ''Death in a Prairie house: Frank Lloyd Wright and the Taliesin Murders'' (University of Wisconsin Press, 2008) p. 163; Anthony Weston, "Return of Thanks", in ''Mobilizing the Green Imagination'' (New Society Publishers, 2012), p. 168.</ref>{{Clarify|date=June 2026}} He is a 1976 [[Latin honors|summa cum laude]] graduate of [[Macalester College]], and received his PhD in philosophy in 1982 from the [[University of Michigan]], where he wrote his PhD dissertation with [[Frithjof Bergmann]] on "The Subjectivity of Values".<ref>University of Michigan Department of Philosophy, Pre-1990 Graduate Placement List, http://www.lsa.umich.edu/philosophy/graduate/placement/pre1990{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He taught at the [[State University of New York at Stony Brook]] for ten years, and subsequently at [[Elon University]], where he was recognized for both teaching and scholarly work,<ref>David Hibbard, "Faculty receive awards at annual luncheon", Elon University E-Net, September 5, 2007,
http://www.elon.edu/e-net/Note.aspx?id=921569</ref> as well as abroad in [[Costa Rica]], [[Western Australia]], and [[British Columbia]].{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}}

Weston has experience in interdisciplinary themes, pedagogy, and other fields of study.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} He has co-taught with biologists and ecologists in both Philosophy and Environmental Studies at Elon,<ref>Secondary Faculty, Department of Environmental Studies, Elon University, http://www.elon.edu/e-web/academics/elon_college/environmental_studies/faculty.xhtml</ref> working as well with astronomers,<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ999210 | doi=10.3847/AER2012033 | title=Experiential Education on the Edge: SETI Activities for the College Classroom | year=2012 | last1=Crider | first1=Anthony | last2=Weston | first2=Anthony | journal=Astronomy Education Review | volume=11 | issue=1 | page=010202 | bibcode=2012AEdRv..11a0202C | doi-access=free | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Zen masters<ref>''Kaihan: Newsletter of the North Carolina Zen Center'', Winter 2009, {{cite web|url=http://www.nczencenter.org/Pages/KaihanPages/Winter%202009.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=February 22, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928013322/http://www.nczencenter.org/Pages/KaihanPages/Winter%202009.pdf |archive-date=September 28, 2013 }}</ref>{{Clarify|date=June 2026}} and in environmental education programs<ref>http://www.royalroads.ca/NR/rdonlyres/DA227F4A-5FCC-40AE-B97E-A9D7712BC156/0/MEEC2008ProgramSchedule3June08.pdf{{dead link|date=October 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> as well as on design and social change projects such as Common Ground [[Ecovillage]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.hartsmill.org/ | title=Hart's Mill Ecovillage & Farm}}</ref> Weston retired from full-time teaching in 2018.

==Philosophical work==
Weston's philosophical project as a whole advances an expansive "toolbox" for critical, creative, and constructive thinking, especially for purposes of social and environmental re-imagination and pragmatic ethical practice.{{Clarify|date=June 2026}} He argues that social, ethical, and [[ontological]] problems that we so often take as "given" are more often then not, products of underlying conditions, practices, and choices.<ref>Ben Hale, Review of Anthony Weston's ''The Incompleat Eco-Philosopher'', in ''Social Theory and Practice'' 38 (2012): 160–164.</ref> This view may be identified with [[deconstruction]]. However, Weston argues:

: "...the genuine promise of this critical move is betrayed by the thinnest of follow-ups. We need to give the same kind of attention to the ''re''-construction of ''genuinely better alternatives'' in the new space of freedom that broadly deconstructive moves create." ("A 21st Century Philosophical Toolbox", Keynote address for the Atlantic Region Philosophers Association Conference, 10/16/09){{Citation needed|date=June 2026|reason=Can't find the original source}}

This line of thinking, which was inspired in particular by the [[Pragmatism|pragmatic]] social philosophy of [[John Dewey]], believed by Weston to encourage open-ended, generative, imaginative, and experimental thinking, is modeled on crafts such as building or performance. It also encourages the displacement of category-bound and formal thinking that tends to be more reactive and critical by [[empirical science]].{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} A key concept of his theory is the idea that while the majority of concepts and objects have much more depth than may appear, thematizing and [[self-validating reduction]] limits the ability to realize this depth.<ref>Jickling, B., Lotz-Sisitka, H., O'Donoghue, R., Ogbuigwe. A. (2006) ''Environmental Education, Ethics, and Action''. Nairobi: UNEP. pp.&nbsp;12–19. http://cjee.lakeheadu.ca/public/journals/22/Ethics_book_english.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426061352/http://cjee.lakeheadu.ca/public/journals/22/Ethics_book_english.pdf |date=April 26, 2012 }}</ref> Correspondingly, he argues, people should not "read off" the nature and possibility of things off the world as it is "given", but instead actively engage with the world, to create new kinds of openings in interaction with the world within which deeper possibilities might emerge.<ref>Jim Cheney, Review of Anthony Weston's ''Back to Earth: Tomorrow's Environmentalism'' in ''Environmental Ethics'' 18 (1996): 91–94.</ref>

He also argues that these issues appear in the "originary" areas of ethics, as Weston calls them. He believes that they are only just beginning to become developed fields. He argues that as such, they can not be "solved" by only the extension or application of pre-given principles, instead requiring the co-creation or co-constitution of new values. In [[environmental ethics]] in particular, Weston argues that it is still a highly theoretical field.<ref>Andrew Light and Eric Katz, ''Environmental Pragmatism'' (Routledge, 1996), pp. 3–4, 10.</ref> He also supports the idea of a multicentric approach to reconstituting the human relation to the [[more-than-human world]], as opposed to an [[anthropocentric]] view or a views "centered" in the sense that one dimension and model for values determines who or what morally counts and why.<ref>Patrick Curry, "Multicentrism", in his ''Ecological Ethics'' (Cambridge, UK: Polity Press, 2011), pp. 156–158.</ref>{{Clarify|reason=Just the last part is a bit confusing|date=June 2026}}

Another important philosophical belief of Weston's relates to the connection of the built and lived world and [[thought]]. Philosophers tend to assume a one-way connection—that thought determines world—while philosophy's critics, such as doctrinaire Marxists, see it just the other way around.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026|reason=I don't think this is accurate. For instance, the blank slate argument is fairly well known idea that directly contradicts the idea that philosophers think thoughts determine world}} In Weston's view, they both influence each other. He claims that the world or a set of concrete practices represent the enactment of certain ideas, but they also shape our ideas in turn. For example, the cultural enactment and perpetuation of anthropocentrism.{{Clarify|reason=I think I might get what this means, but it's a bad example and confusing|date=June 2026}} He believes that, assuming his theory is correct, the dialectical nature of it gives thought an anchor, allows people to work out ideas concretely, and allows for philosophical change:<ref>Christopher Preston, "Environmental Knowledge: Courteous Yet Subversive, Grounded Yet Surprising", ''Ethics, Policy and Environment'' 14 (2011): 91–96. http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/21550085.2011.561601</ref>

: The world shapes our concepts but does not determine them; likewise our concepts shape our thought but do not determine it. The upshot is conceptual room to move. Rather than analyzing concepts as if they were fixed read-offs of reality, we can reshape and relocate them, and by so doing remake thought and the world itself. ("A 21st Century Philosophical Toolbox"){{Citation needed|date=June 2026}}

* "Beyond Intrinsic Value: Pragmatism in Environmental Ethics", ''Environmental Ethics'' 7:4 (1985): 321–339. [http://philpapers.org/rec/WESBIV]
* "Forms of Gaian Ethics", ''Environmental Ethics'' 9:3 (1987): 121–134. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130415140811/http://www.secure.pdcnet.org/enviroethics/content/enviroethics_1987_0009_0003_0217_0230?file_type=pdf}}
* "Radio Astronomy as Epistemology: Some Philosophical Reflections on the [[Search for extraterrestrial intelligence|Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence]]", ''Monist'' 71:1 (1988): 88–100. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130415135636/http://secure.pdcnet.org/monist/content/monist_1988_0071_0001_0088_0100}}
* "Uncovering the 'Hidden Curriculum': A Laboratory Course in Philosophy of Education", ''APA Newsletter on Teaching Philosophy'' 90:2 (Winter 1991): 36–40. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130128103601/http://www.mendeley.com/research/foundations-for-a-philosophy-of-education/}}
* "Non-anthropocentrism in a Thoroughly Anthropocentrized World", ''The Trumpeter'' 8:3 (1991): 108–112. [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110956/http://www.synergiescanada.org/journals/synpra/trumpet/50/459]
* "Before Environmental Ethics", ''Environmental Ethics'' 14 (1992): 323–340 [https://www.pdcnet.org/enviroethics/content/enviroethics_1992_0014_0004_0321_0338]
* "Self-Validating Reduction: Toward a Theory of the Devaluation of Nature", ''Environmental Ethics'' 18 (1996): 115–132. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130415145720/http://www.secure.pdcnet.org/enviroethics/content/enviroethics_1996_0018_0002_0115_0132?file_type=pdf}}
* "Instead of Environmental Education", in Bob Jickling, ed., ''Proceedings of the Yukon College Symposium on Ethics, Environment, and Education'' (Whitehorse, Y.T.: Yukon College, 1996).
*  "Risking Philosophy of Education", ''Metaphilosophy'' 29 (1998): 145–158. [http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1467-9973.00087/abstract]
* "Environmental Ethics as Environmental Etiquette: Toward an Ethics-Based Epistemology in Environmental Philosophy" (with Jim Cheney), ''Environmental Ethics'' 21 (1999): 115–134. [https://web.archive.org/web/20140330112648/http://www.umweltethik.at/download.php?id=398]

==Criticism==
Critics argue that Weston's notions of "originary ethics" and "reconstructive engagement" offer little or no practical application, especially in less-than-optimal situations in which choices nonetheless must be made. Though Weston has challenged what he has called "dilemma-ism" as a method of doing ethics or as an expectation about the necessary structure of ethical problems, genuine dilemmas that need to be addressed do exist. Some critics hold that Weston's vision of opening up new possibilities would open up a range of problematic and disturbing possibilities as well.<ref>Eric Katz, "Envisioning a De-Anthropocentrised World: Critical Comments on Anthony Weston's 'The Incompleat Eco-Philosopher'". ''Ethics, Policy and Environment'' 14: 97–101. http://philpapers.org/rec/KATEAD. Andrew Light, "Environmental Pragmatism as Philosophy or Metaphilosophy? On the Weston-Katz Debate", in Andrew Light and Eric Katz, editors, ''Environmental Pragmatism'' (Routledge, 1996), pp. 325–338.</ref>

Weston's ethics textbooks in particular take substantive positions in ethical philosophy. Weston's rationale is that any practical textbook necessarily does so, and that this is just less noticeable or objectionable to traditionalists in the usual textbooks because the substance tends to be the taken-for-granted norms.<ref>"Notes for Teachers", ''A 21st Century Ethical Toolbox'' (second edition, Oxford University Press, 2008), p. 444.</ref>
